facts.label: Number of participants
Who was enrolled, when, and how steps were measured
facts.quote: This cohort study evaluated a representative sample of participants aged 20 years or older in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys 2005-2006 who wore an accelerometer for 1 week and their mortality data through December 31, 2019.

facts.label: How participants were grouped
facts.quote: Participants were grouped by the number of days per week they took 8000 steps or more (0 days, 1-2 days, and 3-7 days).

facts.label: Length of follow-up and number of deaths
facts.quote: Over the 10-year follow-up, all-cause and cardiovascular deaths occurred in 439 (14.2%) and 148 (5.3%) participants, respectively.

facts.label: What each adjustment model added
facts.value: Model 2 included average daily step counts
facts.quote: Model 1 included age; sex; race and ethnicity; insurance status; marital status; smoking; body mass index; estimated glomerular filtration rate; statin use; and history of diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and emphysema. Model 2 included average daily step counts in addition to the covariates in model 1.

facts.label: Where the curve flattened
facts.quote: the risk of mortality at 10 years rapidly decreased as the number of days per week taking 8000 steps or more increased and plateaued at 3 to 4 days

facts.label: Mean age of the three groups (0, 1-2, 3-7 days)
Number (%) with a mobility limitation in the three groups
How mobility limitation was defined
facts.quote: Mobility limitations were defined as self-report of difficulty walking 0.25 miles without special equipment or climbing 10 stairs.

facts.label: Other step thresholds gave similar results
facts.quote: Different thresholds for the number of daily steps between 6000 and 10 000 yielded similar results.

facts.label: Earlier meta-analysis on steps per day and mortality, cited by the authors
facts.quote: a recent meta-analysis showed decreasing mortality risks with an increasing number of daily steps until 6000 to 8000 steps are reached for adults older than 60 years and at 8000 to 10 000 steps per day for those younger than 60 years

facts.label: Steps measured for a single week
facts.value: daily steps were only measured for 1 week at baseline
facts.quote: because daily steps were only measured for 1 week at baseline, we did not have information on how changes in physical activity contribute to risk of mortality

facts.label: Residual confounding by health status
facts.quote: our findings still have residual confounding bias (ie, poor health could influence daily step counts and mortality risk)

facts.label: People may walk more because they are wearing a tracker
facts.quote: as a result of knowledge that they are wearing the device, participants might have a tendency to be more active, a phenomenon known as the Hawthorne effect
